# AI Research Lab

A reusable workspace for academic literature research. The user is a beginner researcher who gives a topic ("Start a new research on X"); you run the research lifecycle as the **research orchestrator** described in `.claude/agents/research-orchestrator.md` (delegation table and state ownership live there).

## Rules (full version: `docs/research-standards.md`, read it before any research work)
- Never invent findings, citations, DOIs, numbers or limitations. Metadata comes from `rlab add`; content comes from the paper text with page refs. Unknown → say "not reported" / "not found".
- Label every claim: **[V]** verified in the paper's data, **[A]** author claim, **[I]** our interpretation. Cite `[@key, p. N]`.
- Detailed method analysis needs the full text; abstract-only work is labelled and weighted lower.
- Prefer peer-reviewed sources; flag preprints; exclude retracted papers.
- Legal open access only. Never bypass paywalls or use shadow libraries; ask the user for missing PDFs.
- Never overwrite or delete `paper.pdf`, `fulltext.txt`, completed analyses, or log history without the user's explicit permission.
- A research gap is claimed only after a recorded novelty check.

## Tools
- `rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py` (run from this directory; `-h` lists commands). Use it for every deterministic step: project creation, search, adding papers (resolves + verifies metadata, rejects duplicates), PDF fetch/attach + text extraction, validation, BibTeX, citation checks, indexing, logging. Never hand-edit `metadata.json`, `registry.json`, `literature-matrix.*`, `references.bib` or `research/INDEX.md`.
- After changing project content, run `rlab index <id>`; log decisions with `rlab log <id> <phase> "<msg>"`.
- Skills (`.claude/skills/`): start-research, discover-papers, analyze-paper, compare-methods, find-gaps, write-literature-review, research-report, reading-guide, resume-research.
- Shareable Google Doc: `python3 scripts/md2gdoc.py --title T --subtitle S [--share anyone] [--pdf out.pdf] [--md out.md] a.md b.md ...` turns simple markdown (one file per page; see the script docstring) into a styled Google Doc owned by the user (auth via the google-doc-builder skill). Per-project reading guides live in `reports/reading-guide/` (`00-front.md`, `papers/<key>.md`, `99-back.md`, `order.txt`).
- External services in use: OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv, PubMed, doi.org, Europe PMC (no keys needed). Semantic Scholar is rate-limited without a key: use it via WebFetch only as a fallback. Unpaywall runs only if `RLAB_CONTACT_EMAIL` is set.

## Layout
- `research/registry.json` — all projects (via `rlab`); `research/INDEX.md` — human overview.
- `research/<id>/` — one project: `RESEARCH.md`, `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`, `STATUS.md`, `research-log.md`, `literature-matrix.md/.csv`, `evidence-matrix.md`, `gap-report.md`, `references.bib`, `search/`, `papers/<key>/{metadata.json,paper.pdf,fulltext.txt,analysis.md,paper.bib}`, `reports/`.
- `templates/` — project and analysis templates. `docs/` — standards. `tests/` — `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests`.

## Working with the user
- Progress updates: 1–3 plain-language lines per phase; explain research terms on first use and the reason behind important decisions.
- Handle routine work yourself. Ask only for: scope/RQ choices that change direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, destructive actions.
- State lives in files, not in conversation memory: keep `STATUS.md` (Next actions, Blocked / needs user) current so any session can resume.
- [Reading guide doc preference](reading-guide-doc-preference.md) — end every project with plain-English reading guide as public-link Google Doc

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications that cut a real corner with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic) with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and upgrade path (`# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`).

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

# Research standards

The rules every skill and agent in this workspace follows. One source of truth: change rules here, not in individual skills.

## 1. Evidence labels
Every substantive statement about a paper or the literature carries one label:

| Label | Short | Meaning | Requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| VERIFIED | [V] | Checked against the paper's own data, tables, figures or results text. | Page ref `(key, p. N)` |
| AUTHOR-CLAIM | [A] | The authors state it; we cannot independently check it (e.g. claims of novelty, interpretations, conclusions beyond the data). | Page ref |
| INTERPRETATION | [I] | Our own reasoning, synthesis or critique. | Say what it is based on |

Page refs use the `=== [PDF page N] ===` markers in `fulltext.txt` (PDF page index, not printed page number). When a quote is used, it is copied verbatim from `fulltext.txt`.

Citation syntax:
- Inside a paper's own `analysis.md`: `(p. N)`.
- Everywhere else (evidence matrix, reports, reviews): pandoc style `[@key, p. N]` or `[@key1; @key2]`. Keys are the folder names under `papers/`. This works with `references.bib` and pandoc.
- `rlab cite-check <project> <file...>` must pass before any written document is handed to the user.

## 2. Never invent
- Every DOI, title, author, year and venue comes from `metadata.json` (resolved by `rlab add` from Crossref/OpenAlex/arXiv/PubMed). Never type a DOI from memory.
- Every finding, number, limitation and quote comes from the paper text. If the paper does not report something, write "not reported".
- Every citation in written output uses an existing paper key in the project. A claim with no source is either removed or labelled [I].
- If something cannot be found or verified, say so plainly. An honest "unknown" beats a plausible guess.

## 3. Source quality tiers
Prefer higher tiers; state the tier when it matters to the argument.

1. Peer-reviewed journal articles and full papers at reputable conferences (`venue_kind: published`); systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top for evidence synthesis.
2. Peer-reviewed workshop papers, book chapters from academic publishers.
3. Preprints (`venue_kind: preprint`, e.g. arXiv): usable, always flagged "not peer-reviewed". If a published version exists, use it instead.
4. Theses, technical reports, grey literature: background only, flagged.
5. Blogs, news, Wikipedia, vendor material: never cited as evidence. May guide searching.

`venue_kind: published` means the work appeared in a journal or proceedings; it is not proof of rigorous review. Watch for predatory venues (unknown publisher, implausibly fast review, no indexing) and flag them.
Retracted papers (`RETRACTED` flag from `rlab`) are excluded from evidence; mention only as retracted.

## 4. Reading depth
- Detailed methodology, dataset, setup, metrics, findings and limitations require the full text (`evidence_basis: full-text`).
- Abstract-only analysis (`evidence_basis: abstract-only`) may fill objective and headline claims labelled [A] only. All method sections say "full text not available". Abstract-only papers carry less weight in synthesis and gap claims; say so.
- Read the whole paper: methods, results, tables, limitations, appendix if relevant. Note skipped parts in "Analyst notes".

## 5. Critical appraisal checklist
For every empirical paper check and record:
- Sample size and how it was chosen; power or uncertainty reporting.
- Baselines and whether they are fair and current.
- Evaluation design: train/test separation, leakage, cross-validation, held-out data, blinding, control groups.
- Statistical testing: tests, effect sizes, confidence intervals, multiple comparisons.
- Reproducibility: data, code, hyper-parameters, protocol available?
- Conflicts of interest and funding where relevant.
- Whether conclusions go beyond the data (mark those [A] and note it).

Evidence strength: **strong** = adequate N, sound design, replicated or consistent across studies; **moderate** = sound design but single study or limited N; **weak** = small/unclear N, design flaws, abstract-only, or preprint without replication.

## 6. Contradictions
When papers disagree: record both sides in the evidence matrix "Contradictions" section with page refs, then compare data, population, method, metric and time. Offer an explanation only as [I]. Never silently pick a side.

## 7. Research gaps and novelty
A gap is reported only when:
1. It is supported by evidence from analysed papers (explicit future-work statements, consistent limitations, contradictions, untested populations/conditions, missing method comparisons).
2. A dedicated novelty check was run: at least 3 targeted searches (`rlab search`) across at least 2 sources, recent years included, plus a web search for very recent work. Queries, date and closest hits are recorded in the gap entry.
3. Confidence is stated. "No paper found" is phrased as "we found no paper that ... (searches on DATE)", never "this has never been studied".

## 8. Copyright and access
- Download only legal open-access copies: OpenAlex/Unpaywall OA locations, arXiv, Europe PMC, publisher OA pages. `rlab fetch` enforces this and refuses shadow libraries.
- Never bypass paywalls, logins, CAPTCHAs, or rate limits. Never use Sci-Hub, LibGen, Anna's Archive or similar.
- When no OA copy exists: tell the user and ask them to obtain it through their library, then `rlab attach`. Otherwise analyse abstract-only and label it.
- Quotes stay short and attributed. PDFs stay inside the project folder and are not redistributed.

## 9. Preservation
- Original PDFs (`paper.pdf`), extracted text (`fulltext.txt`) and completed analyses (`status: complete`) are never overwritten or deleted without the user's explicit permission. A hook asks the user first (once `setup/claude-settings.json` is installed).
- Analysis status flow: `draft` (in progress) -> `ready` (analyst self-check passed) -> `complete` (critical review passed). Fix review findings while the analysis is `ready`.
- Revisions to a completed analysis go in a new section `## Revision YYYY-MM-DD` with what changed and why, after the user agrees.
- `research-log.md` is append-only.

## 10. Talking to the user (a beginner researcher)
- Progress updates: short, what was done, what was found, what is next.
- Explain research terms on first use in one plain sentence (e.g. "a *systematic review* is a study that collects and evaluates all studies on a question").
- Explain important decisions and their reason: scope cuts, exclusions, weak evidence, gaps.
- Ask only for: scope or research-question choices that change the direction, missing full-text access, paid or restricted resources, and anything destructive.

name: analyze-paper
description: Analyse one research paper in depth (objective, method, data, setup, metrics, findings, limitations, validity threats, future work, relevance) with page-cited evidence. Use when a project paper needs its analysis.md written or completed.
---

# Analyse a paper

`rlab` = `python3 scripts/rlab.py`. Rules: [docs/research-standards.md](../../../docs/research-standards.md) — labels §1, never invent §2, reading depth §4, appraisal checklist §5.

Input: project id + paper key. Files live in `research/<id>/papers/<key>/`.

## 1. Prepare
- `rlab scaffold <id> <key>` (creates `analysis.md`; never overwrites an existing one).
- Read `metadata.json`. Note `venue_kind`, `is_retracted`, `fulltext.status`, `fulltext.identity`, `fulltext.text_layer`.
- `identity` UNCONFIRMED → read PDF page 1 and confirm it is this paper; if not, stop and report.
- `text_layer` POOR → read pages from `paper.pdf` with the Read tool (`pages` parameter) instead of `fulltext.txt`.
- No full text → `evidence_basis: abstract-only`; fill objective and headline claims as [A] from the abstract in `metadata.json`, write "full text not available" in sections 3–6, 8 and 10, and stop at step 4.

## 2. Read the whole paper
Read `fulltext.txt` in chunks (Read with offset/limit) from start to end: abstract, introduction, method, results, tables, discussion, limitations, conclusion. Use Grep for `limitation|threat|future work|we did not|sample|dataset|N =` to make sure nothing is missed. For tables or figures garbled by text extraction, read that PDF page directly. Page numbers come from the nearest preceding `=== [PDF page N] ===` marker.

## 3. Write the analysis
Fill every section of `analysis.md`. Each [V]/[A] item ends with `(p. N)`. Use "not reported" when the paper is silent — that absence is itself useful information (e.g. no sample size reported). Separate author-stated limitations (section 8, [A]) from limitations you identify (section 9, [I]). Apply the appraisal checklist to section 10. Fill the evidence table (section 13) with rows linked to project RQ ids from `RESEARCH-QUESTIONS.md`.

## 4. Frontmatter
Fill the single-line frontmatter fields: `design`, `dataset`, `sample_size`, `metrics`, `main_finding` (≤25 words), `relevance` (high/medium/low). These feed the literature matrix.

## 5. Self-check
- Every [V]/[A] has a page ref; `rlab cite-check <id> research/<id>/papers/<key>/analysis.md` passes.
- Grep `fulltext.txt` for 3 of your quotes/numbers: each is found on the cited page.
- No template placeholder or empty required section remains.
Then set `status: ready` and run `rlab index <id>`.

Done when: `status: ready` and the self-check passed — or `status: draft` with the blocking reason written in "Analyst notes".

## 6. Return
Report: key, 2-line summary, evidence-table rows, anything surprising (contradicts other work, suspicious results, missing data).
# Research questions — LLM-based vs Traditional Static Analysis and Deep Learning Approaches for Source Code Vulnerability Detection: A Comparative Review

<!-- 3-5 questions. Each must be answerable from literature evidence. -->

## RQ1: How do LLM-based approaches compare with SAST tools and DL detectors in detection effectiveness (precision, recall, F1, false-positive rate) in head-to-head evaluations?
- Type: comparative
- Why it matters: the core practical question — which approach finds more real vulnerabilities with fewer false alarms.
- Linked objective: 1
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12)
- Current answer: No family wins across settings. Frontier LLMs beat SAST on small, self-contained code [@gnieciak2025large, p. 10; @dubniczky2025castle, p. 11], but CodeQL beats LLMs on synthetic function-level suites [@khare2025understanding, p. 9]. At project scale general coding agents reach far higher recall than SAST (59.55% vs 0–34.29% on C/C++) while most LLM detectors and SAST tools produce mostly false warnings [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 11]. Versus fine-tuned DL the ranking depends on dataset and class balance [@fu2023chatgpt, p. 4; @shu2026evaluating, p. 40], and all families are near or below chance on PrimeVul pairs [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9; @tan2026think, p. 6]. **Strength: weak–moderate.** Most robust pattern [I]: LLMs have higher recall, lower precision.

## RQ2: How do evaluation setups (benchmarks, languages, CWE coverage, synthetic vs. real-world code, data-leakage control) differ across studies, and how do they explain disagreements in reported results?
- Type: methodological
- Why it matters: results that look contradictory may come from different benchmarks; this decides how much any number can be trusted.
- Linked objective: 2
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12)
- Current answer: Evaluation setup explains much of the disagreement: label noise (39–65% correct) [@risse2025top, p. 8], exact-copy leakage up to 18.9% [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 4], balanced vs realistic class ratios that flip rankings [@shu2026evaluating, p. 40; @yildiz2025benchmarking, p. 7], synthetic vs real code [@khare2025understanding, p. 5], function vs statement granularity [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 8], and custom datasets with inconsistent splits [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 35]. **Strength: moderate–strong** (consistent across independent primary studies and two SLRs).

## RQ3: Do hybrid LLM + static-analysis approaches outperform either family alone, and what are the trade-offs in cost, speed and explainability?
- Type: comparative
- Why it matters: industry is moving to combined tools; evidence for their benefit is scattered.
- Linked objective: 3
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12)
- Current answer: LLM filtering of SAST alarms removes most false alarms at < $0.20 per alarm but loses 12–25% of real bugs [@du2026reducing, p. 8; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18] (**moderate**). Hybrid detection (IRIS, RepoAudit) beats SAST in the authors' own evaluations [@li2024iris, p. 8; @guo2025repoaudit, p. 8] but not in an independent project-scale study [@li2026llm, p. 7; @li2026llm, p. 12], and needs a strong LLM [@li2024iris, p. 10] (**weak/contested**). LLM costs range from cents per alarm to $1,247.66 per project vs minutes and no token cost for SAST [@li2026llm, p. 16]. Explainability is limited: LLMs mislocate findings [@gnieciak2025large, p. 11] and fluent explanations do not signal correctness [@tan2026think, p. 9].

## RQ4: Which vulnerability types (CWEs), languages and code scales does each family handle well or poorly?
- Type: comparative
- Why it matters: guides tool choice for a given codebase and points to where research is missing.
- Linked objective: 1, 4
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12)
- Current answer: LLMs do best on self-contained injection-style CWEs and worst on context-dependent and crypto/policy CWEs and on localising memory-safety bugs [@khare2025understanding, p. 7; @xiong2026sifting, p. 18; @shu2026evaluating, p. 30]; CodeQL is better on CWE-190 [@khare2025understanding, p. 8]. LLM performance falls with function/file length [@ahmed2026secvuleval, p. 13; @li2026llm, p. 9]; evidence is concentrated on C/C++ and Java [@kaniewski2026systematic, p. 28]. **Strength: weak** (small per-CWE cells, divergent results).

## RQ5: What gaps and open problems remain for reliable, deployable LLM-based vulnerability detection?
- Type: descriptive
- Why it matters: basis for the gap section and future work of the paper.
- Linked objective: 4
- Status: answered (synthesis 2026-11-12)
- Current answer: Recurring open problems: verified, realistic, repository-level benchmarks with context [@zhou2025large, p. 19; @sheng2025llms, p. 25]; same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs DL comparisons (only khare runs all three, SAST on synthetic data only [@khare2025understanding, p. 7]); independent labelling and statistical testing [@li2026llm, p. 11]; cost reporting; contamination control; true-positive loss in filtering [@xiong2026sifting, p. 19]; workflow integration [@zhou2025large, p. 19]. **Strength: moderate** [I]. Candidate gaps until novelty-checked in gap-report.md.

  "title": "A Review of Source Code Vulnerability Detection Methods Based on Large Language Models: Models, Techniques, and Evaluation",
  "authors": [
    {
      "family": "Qin",
      "given": "Letong"
    }
  ],
  "year": 2026,
  "venue": "Computers and Artificial Intelligence",
  "type": "journal-article",
  "venue_kind": "published",
  "doi": "10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137",

  "openalex_id": "W7224195243",

  "is_oa": true,

  "cited_by": 0,
  "abstract": "In source code vulnerability detection, large language models (LLMs) are no longer used only as substitutes for traditional fixed classifiers. With prompt design, parameter fine-tuning, and program-context information, they can judge whether code contains vulnerabilities and can also provide suspicious locations and explanatory evidence. This paper takes lightweight code Transformers and large-scale language models as two main lines of discussion. It reviews methods for input construction, task adaptation, the use of program-analysis information, and multi-model collaboration, and compares them in terms of datasets, evaluation metrics, and deployment conditions. Existing studies show that code pretraining, prompt engineering, supervised fine-tuning, and structural-information enhancement can improve detection or explanation results on specific benchmarks. However, such improvements are easily affected by duplicate samples, label noise, random splits, temporal leakage, and changes in model versions, which may lead to overestimated performance. Therefore, model evaluation should not rely on a single metric alone. It should also report the data source, detection granularity, temporal or project-level isolation, false-positive cost, and whether generated explanations can be verified by program evidence. On this basis, this paper further discusses an application approach centered on data governance, strict data splitting, uncertainty calibration, and SAST-LLM-human collaboration. The discussion is limited to source-code-level vulnerability detection, localization, and classification, and does not cover network intrusion detection, malware analysis, smart-contract-specific detection, vulnerability generation, or automatic repair.",
  "sources": [
    "crossref",
    "openalex"
  ],
  "key": "qin2026review",
  "added": "2026-11-12T09:40:28+06:00",
  "added_reason": "Closest competing review (CAI 2026); positioning — must be cited (gap-report)",
  "found_via": "gap novelty check: review LLM vs traditional vulnerability detection evaluation pitfalls",
  "verification": {
    "status": "verified",
    "checked": "2026-11-12T17:43:59+06:00",
    "cross_checks": {

1	---
     2	key: qin2026review
     3	status: ready
     4	evidence_basis: full-text
     5	design: narrative (non-systematic) literature review, single author; no search protocol or quality assessment
     6	dataset: none (secondary); 32 cited references, 2019-2026
     7	sample_size: 32 references (no stated corpus of primary studies)
     8	metrics: none (qualitative synthesis; re-reports P/R/F1, VD-S, Top-k, Effort@Recall from cited papers)

    13	<!-- Frontmatter: single-line values; they feed literature-matrix.md via `rlab index`.
    14	     status: draft (in progress) -> ready (analyst self-check passed) -> complete (critical review passed).

    17	
    18	# A Review of Source Code Vulnerability Detection Methods Based on Large Language Models: Models, Techniques, and Evaluation
    19	
    20	- Authors: Qin, Letong
    21	- Year / venue: 2026, Computers and Artificial Intelligence (published)
    22	- DOI: 10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137 · URL: https://doi.org/10.70267/cai.v3n5.122137
    23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    24	
    25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
    27	
    28	## 1. Research objective
    29	- [A] Review source-code vulnerability detection with "lightweight code Transformers and large-scale language models" as the two lines of discussion, covering input construction, task adaptation, use of program-analysis information and multi-model collaboration, and compare them by datasets, metrics and deployment conditions (p. 1).
    30	- [A] Scope is limited to source-code-level detection, localization and classification; network intrusion, malware, smart contracts, vulnerability generation and automatic repair are excluded (p. 1).
    31	
    32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    33	- [A] Three organising questions in the introduction: what capabilities methods actually improve, under what data conditions/protocols the gains are obtained, and whether evidence suffices for real-world deployment (p. 2).
    34	- [A] Four formal RQs: RQ1 development from sequence/graph models to code pretraining and LLM interaction; RQ2 performance evidence of direct prompting, in-context learning, fine-tuning, structural enhancement and multi-model collaboration; RQ3 effects of label noise, duplication, class imbalance and temporal leakage; RQ4 how cross-project, out-of-time, false-positive-cost, localization and explanation evaluation approach deployment (p. 4).
    35	- [I] The paper is internally inconsistent here: the introduction speaks of "three closely related questions" (p. 2) while Section 3.1 sets four RQs (p. 4). It also gives "medium confidence to C2" (p. 12) although no claims C1/C2 are defined anywhere in the text.
    36	
    37	## 3. Methodology
    38	- Research design: [I] Narrative (traditional) review. The paper calls itself a "review" (p. 1) and gives no search strategy, databases, search strings, date window, inclusion/exclusion screening, PRISMA flow, or study-quality assessment — all "not reported". The only inclusion rule stated is that it "includes only studies that directly analyze source code" and excludes repair (p. 4).
    39	- Approach / taxonomy: [A] Methods are classified "by how vulnerability knowledge is acquired" rather than by model scale, core technology or supply-chain stage as in earlier reviews (p. 4). Two routes: (a) lightweight code Transformers — code pretraining + supervised fine-tuning, input granularity, structural fusion (pp. 5–6); (b) large-scale LLMs — supervised fine-tuning/steering, multitask learning, direct prompting, few-shot/ICL, hybrid detection with program analysis, ensembles/multi-model collaboration, explanation (pp. 6–9). Figure 1 adds cross-cutting layers "Data and bias", "Reliability evaluation" and "Discussion and outlook" (p. 3) [V, from figure].
    40	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [A] Traditional methods (SAST, GNNs) are discussed "only in two situations": to motivate structural information for Transformers and as baselines or external tools for LLMs; "this paper does not provide a separate review of traditional detection methods" (p. 4). Section 7.1 nevertheless compares LLMs with DL and SAST qualitatively (pp. 11–12).
    41	
    42	## 4. Dataset and sample
    43	- Data source(s): [V] Secondary literature; the reference list has 32 entries (pp. 14–16).
    44	- Sample size (N) and unit: [I] No corpus size is stated; we counted 32 references (pp. 14–16), of which roughly a dozen are LLM-based detection studies (Table 1 lists 11 representative methods, pp. 6–7). Several references are themselves reviews/surveys [2–4, 18–21] (pp. 14–15).
    45	- Sampling / selection method: not reported. [I] Reference years run 2019–2026 (pp. 14–16), but no time window is stated. Figure 2 places milestones from 2019 (Devign) to 2026 (context enhancement, M2CVD) (p. 4) [V, from figure].
    46	- Data availability: not applicable / not reported (no extraction sheet or study list released).
    47	
    48	## 5. Experimental setup
    49	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: not applicable (no experiments). [V] One quantitative re-analysis: the review re-reads PrimeVul Table V for five code LMs — BigVul train/test F1 62.88%–68.26%, BigVul→PrimeVul F1 1.91%–5.82%, PrimeVul train/test F1 18.05%–21.43%, paired-both-correct 1.06%–3.01% (p. 12). [I] We checked these numbers against the PrimeVul text in this project (ding2025vulnerability, p. 7, Table V); the 68.26%/3.09% pair matches.
    50	- Code availability: not applicable.
    51	
    52	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    53	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [A] The review recommends reporting at least Precision, Recall, F1 and a confusion matrix, grouped by project, time, language or CWE; Top-k and audit effort at fixed recall for localization; separate checks of location/type/cause/suggestion for explanations; Accuracy only as supplementary; mean, fluctuation range and parse-failure rate for repeated LLM calls (p. 11). It re-reports VD-Score and paired metrics from PrimeVul (p. 11) and Top-10 Accuracy/Effort@20%Recall from LineVul (p. 5).
    54	- Statistical testing: not applicable; the review does no pooling, meta-analysis or effect-size synthesis (not reported).
    55	
    56	## 7. Key findings
    57	1. Benchmark inflation — [A] Gains from code pretraining, prompting, fine-tuning and structural enhancement hold "on specific benchmarks" but are "easily affected by duplicate samples, label noise, random splits, temporal leakage, and changes in model versions" (p. 1). Supported by the PrimeVul re-reading: StarCoder2 F1 68.26% on BigVul vs 3.09% on the PrimeVul test set (p. 2) and the five-model ranges above (p. 12).
    58	2. Random-split F1 should be called "within-benchmark performance", not a real-world detection rate; out-of-time testing should be a reliability baseline, combined with project isolation and reporting of time windows, data-freeze dates and model knowledge cutoffs (p. 10) — [A].
    59	3. Contamination from pretraining corpora is treated "as an alternative explanation that needs to be audited", not a confirmed fact; knowledge-cutoff dates are not proof of no contamination (p. 10) — [A].
    60	4. Cross-study ranking is not possible: GRACE, DLAP, context enhancement and M2CVD "all report gains in their own settings, but datasets, model versions, and evaluation protocols differ, so they cannot be directly ranked" (p. 12) — [A]. Table 2 gives a risk matrix (label noise, exact/near duplicates, pretraining contamination, random splitting, cross-project/language failure, class imbalance, false-positive cost, explanation/version validity) with identification signals and mitigations (pp. 10–11) — [V, table content].
    61	5. LLM vs SAST vs DL — [A] "SAST is usually more stable within the scope covered by existing rules, whereas LLMs are better at semantic summarization and alert explanation"; unified benchmarks "support complementarity rather than complete replacement", with the two tool types finding different vulnerabilities and different false positives (p. 12), citing a SAST study [1] and the Gnieciak & Szandala LLM-vs-SAST benchmark [15] (p. 15). No numbers for this comparison are given.
    62	6. Hybrids — [A] Proposed workflow: "SAST candidate generation-LLM review or explanation-human confirmation" (p. 8), to be judged by audit time, false-negative control and explanation consistency rather than overall F1 (p. 8); outputs should not be "simply concatenate[d]" (p. 13). Evidence cited is GRACE (structure + ICL, ≥28.65% relative F1 gain over six baselines, p. 8), DLAP (DL-augmented prompting, p. 8) and the context-enhancement study [29] (p. 8). No quantitative evidence on SAST+LLM hybrids is reported.
    63	7. Cost — [A] API calls, GPU memory, latency, model updates and prompt maintenance should be counted; sensitive code and local large-scale scanning suit lightweight models or SAST; high-risk scenarios should use hybrid workflows with human confirmation (p. 12). No cost figures are reported.
    64	8. Re-reported primary numbers (all [A], from cited papers): LineVul 188k+ functions, F1 +160%–379% over baselines, Top-10 Accuracy +12%–25%, Effort@20%Recall −29%–53% (p. 5); DiverseVul 7,514 commits, 18,945 vulnerable / 330,492 non-vulnerable functions, 150 CWEs (p. 9); LLMVulExp average F1 92.4% on SeVC single-type setting (p. 8).
    65	
    66	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
    67	- [A] No separate limitations section. Scope exclusions: network intrusion, malware, smart contracts, generation, repair (p. 1).
    68	- [A] Traditional detection methods are not reviewed separately (p. 4).
    69	- [A] Specific caveats on cited evidence: the PrimeVul conclusion "is limited to the five models and three settings in Table V" (p. 12); LLMVulExp results "cannot be directly generalized to PrimeVul, cross-project testing, or real deployment" (pp. 8–9); GRACE gain is relative and applies only to the tested configurations (p. 8).
    70	
    71	## 9. Limitations we identified
    72	- [I] Not systematic: no search protocol, databases, screening, corpus count or quality assessment (absence across pp. 1–4). Its conclusions cannot be checked for selection bias, and it cannot be cited as a systematic review.
    73	- [I] Small and selective corpus (32 references, pp. 14–16). Missing, among others, project-scale LLM/SAST studies and LLM-based SAST-alarm filtering work that we have (e.g. li2026llm, du2026reducing, xiong2026sifting, li2024iris, guo2025repoaudit); hybrid claims rest on GRACE, DLAP and one context-enhancement study (p. 8), not on SAST+LLM evaluations.
    74	- [I] SAST is explicitly out of scope (p. 4), yet the review draws an LLM-vs-SAST conclusion (p. 12) from two references [1, 15] with no numbers. That conclusion is under-supported.
    75	- [I] Contradictions are explained only in general terms. Apart from the PrimeVul Table V re-reading (p. 12), it does not tabulate conflicting results from different studies side by side against their evaluation setups (benchmark, split, class ratio, granularity). Table 1 (pp. 6–7) is qualitative: no numbers, no split type per study.
    76	- [I] Cites PrimeVul as a 2024 arXiv preprint (p. 15) and leans heavily on that one study for the inflation argument.
    77	- [I] Editorial inconsistencies (three vs four RQs, undefined "C2", p. 2, p. 4, p. 12) suggest light editorial review (see Analyst notes on venue).
    78	
    79	## 10. Threats to validity
    80	- Internal (selection): [I] Unknown selection process, so selection bias cannot be judged; the reviewer's framing (evaluation pitfalls) may have driven which studies were cited.
    81	- External: [I] Mostly C/C++ function-level benchmarks (BigVul, PrimeVul, DiverseVul, SeVC, ReVeal, FFmpeg+Qemu; pp. 8–9, 12); multilingual evidence is one reference [32] (p. 13).
    82	- Construct: [I] Good conceptual separation of label correctness, localization and explanation evidence (p. 4); recommends metrics beyond F1 (p. 11).
    83	- Statistical conclusion: [I] No quantitative synthesis; confidence levels ("medium confidence to C2", p. 12) are given without a stated grading scheme.
    84	- Reproducibility: [I] Not reproducible as a review (no protocol, no study list beyond references).
    85	
    86	## 11. Future research directions
    87	- Stated by authors [A]: traceable data pipelines with commit, time, label-source and duplicate statistics and updateable data cards (p. 13); out-of-time and project-isolated testing as main evidence, random splits only for historical comparison (p. 13); uncertainty calibration, risk-coverage curves and recall at a fixed false-positive budget (p. 13); decomposed verification of explanations (location, trigger, path, CWE, fix) (p. 13); human-machine studies recording audit time per real vulnerability (p. 13); SAST-LLM systems that measure candidate recall, LLM filtering gain, explanation correctness and total audit cost separately (p. 13); preserving system prompts, model IDs, call dates, temperatures and repetition counts (p. 13).
    88	- Suggested by us [I]: a systematic, protocol-based review that puts SAST, DL and LLM results on the same evaluation-setup axes. This is exactly the gap between this review and ours.
    89	
    90	## 12. Relevance to our research
    91	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2 (primary), RQ3 (conceptual only), RQ1 (qualitative only), RQ5.
    92	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the closest competing review and must be cited for positioning. Overlap: evaluation-reliability framing (duplicates, label noise, temporal splits, contamination) and the SAST-LLM-human workflow recommendation. Difference: it is narrative, has a small corpus (32 references), explicitly excludes SAST as a reviewed family, gives no quantitative LLM-vs-SAST or hybrid evidence, and does not map contradictions study-by-study onto evaluation setup. Our contribution should be stated against those four points. Its recommendations corroborate our RQ2 answer independently, but at weak strength.
    93	
    94	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
    95	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
    96	|---|---|---|---|---|
    97	| RQ2 | Benchmark gains are inflated by duplicates, label noise, random splits, temporal leakage and model-version changes; random-split F1 = "within-benchmark performance" only | 1, 10 | A | weak (narrative review) |
    98	| RQ2 | Re-reads PrimeVul Table V: five code LMs F1 62.88–68.26% on BigVul vs 1.91–5.82% BigVul→PrimeVul vs 18.05–21.43% PrimeVul→PrimeVul | 12 | A | moderate (secondary report of a single primary study; numbers match ding2025vulnerability) |
    99	| RQ2 | LLM methods (GRACE, DLAP, context enhancement, M2CVD) cannot be ranked because datasets, model versions and protocols differ | 12 | A | weak |
   100	| RQ1 | SAST more stable within rule coverage; LLMs better at semantic summarisation/explanation; unified benchmarks support complementarity, not replacement (no numbers) | 12 | A | weak |
   101	| RQ3 | Recommends SAST candidates → LLM ranking/explanation → human confirmation; judge by audit time, false negatives, explanation consistency, not F1 | 8, 13 | A | weak (no quantitative hybrid evidence) |
   102	| RQ3 | Costs (API calls, GPU memory, latency, version drift, prompt maintenance) should be reported; none quantified | 9, 12 | A | weak |
   103	| RQ5 | Open problems: out-of-time + project-isolated testing, data cards, uncertainty calibration, fixed-FP-budget recall, explanation verification, audit-time studies | 13 | A | weak |
   104	
   105	## 14. Key quotes
   106	> "this paper does not provide a separate review of traditional detection methods" (p. 4)
   107	
   108	> "Existing evidence from unified benchmarks supports complementarity rather than complete replacement by one tool" (p. 12)
   109	
   110	> "F1 obtained from a random split should be called “within-benchmark performance” and cannot be directly described as a “real-world detection rate”" (p. 10)
   111	
   112	## Analyst notes
   113	- Reading coverage: all 16 PDF pages read in full, including references, funding and copyright notes (pp. 14–16). Figures 1–2 (pp. 3–4) read from the PDF images because pdftotext dropped them.
   114	- Venue quality [I]: Computers and Artificial Intelligence, Vol. 3 No. 5 (2026), E-ISSN 3006-3728, published by "Zeus Press" (p. 1). The PDF has no received/revised/accepted dates and no editor or peer-review statement (pp. 1–16). OpenAlex (queried 2026-11-12) lists the source with no host organisation, `is_in_doaj: false`, `is_core: false`, no indexing lists, and publication date 2026-10-29; cited_by 0 in metadata. The acknowledgment reads only "This paper is an output of the science project." (p. 16). There is a single author, and internal inconsistencies (three vs four RQs; undefined "C2") remain. Together these are warning signs of a low-visibility venue with uncertain peer review. We did not confirm that it is predatory. Treat it as tier 1 by `venue_kind` but weight it like grey literature. Cite it for positioning, not as evidence.
   115	- Competitor positioning [I]: SAST tools are covered only as baselines/external tools, not reviewed (p. 4). Hybrids are covered conceptually (pp. 8, 13), with no SAST+LLM empirical studies. Cross-study contradictions are explained via evaluation setup in general terms and through one worked example (PrimeVul, p. 12), not systematically.
   116	- Uncertainties: whether a systematic search was done but simply not reported. Numbers it gives for other papers are labelled [A] here; only the PrimeVul numbers were cross-checked against a primary text.

improved labeling, and temporal splitting, the PrimeVul study reported that the same StarCoder2 model

1.3    Research Questions and Main Contributions
    This paper is organized around three closely related questions: what capabilities existing methods actually
improve, under what data conditions and evaluation protocols these improvements are obtained, and whether
the available evidence is sufficient to support deployment in real-world scenarios. Cross-project studies,
unified comparisons between LLMs and SAST, and analyses related to DiverseVul all indicate that whether a
tested project has been seen before, differences in programming languages, vulnerability category composition,
and changes in tool versions can affect evaluation results [15-17]. Therefore, this paper first introduces the
necessary background, then defines the tasks and analytical framework. It then discusses lightweight

5.2   Prompt Engineering and In-Context Learning
5.2.1 Direct Prompting
   Direct prompting organizes code and security questions into natural-language instructions and asks a
general-purpose LLM to give a judgment or explanation. Early studies mainly test the feasibility of GPT-like
models without task fine-tuning and also compare joint vulnerability and functionality judgments and different
input modes [10,27-28]. This method adapts quickly to new output formats, but results are easily affected by
prompt wording, context length, and model version, and repeated calls may produce inconsistent answers.

6.3     Evaluation Metrics
   Different classification metrics reflect different questions. Precision focuses on how many alerts produced
by the model are truly credible, Recall focuses on how many real vulnerabilities are found, and F1 takes the
harmonic mean of the two. When vulnerability data are highly imbalanced, reporting Accuracy alone can easily
hide errors on the minority class. For this reason, PrimeVul introduces paired samples, VD-Score, and other
checks that are closer to the vulnerability identification process. Studies on SAST also point out that both rule
coverage and the number of false positives affect practical usability [1,14].
   Evaluation for deployment should also convert model alerts into audit workload. LineVul uses Top-k
Accuracy and Effort@20%Recall to measure the priority of localization results. A unified LLM-SAST
benchmark compares both vulnerability detection and false positives, showing that the two kinds of tools may
complement each other on different vulnerability types [5,15]. For generative explanations, it is not enough to
check whether the text is complete. It is also necessary to examine whether the vulnerability location, causal
explanation, and repair suggestion are consistent with the code. LLMVulExp reflects this extended evaluation
direction, but automatic metrics, human annotation protocols, and consistency standards for explanation
evaluation still need further unification [6].
   Therefore, an evaluation report should at least include Precision, Recall, F1, and a confusion matrix, and
should provide grouped results by project, time, programming language, or CWE type. For line-level
localization methods, Top-k results and the amount of code that needs to be audited under a fixed recall should
also be reported. For generative explanations, location, type, cause, and suggestion should be checked
separately against program evidence. Accuracy can only be used as a supplementary metric. If an experiment
calls an LLM multiple times, it should also report the mean results, fluctuation range, and parsing failure rate.

7.    Comparison of Method Performance and Applicability

7.1     Comparison with Deep Learning and SAST
   Studies on prompting and fine-tuning do provide evidence of performance improvement on public datasets,
but these gains are not fixed. They vary with model type, dataset, parameter configuration, and training budget

   Low scores under strict evaluation do not mean that LLMs have no value in vulnerability detection. A more
important lesson from PrimeVul is that the evaluation protocol itself can change experimental conclusions; the
single result of 3.09% cannot be directly generalized to all models. Conversely, high scores on SeVC or BigVul
cannot simply be treated as detection capability in production environments. In other words, current evidence
shows that model capability has indeed improved, while also exposing insufficient external validity. Both
points need to be retained.

When comparing lightweight Transformers with general-purpose LLMs, model scale is not the only
criterion. Lightweight Transformers are more suitable for scenarios with fixed label systems, local batch
processing, and lockable versions. General-purpose LLMs are more convenient for few-shot adaptation,
explanation generation, and complex context processing. SAST is usually more stable within the scope covered
by existing rules, whereas LLMs are better at semantic summarization and alert explanation. Existing evidence
from unified benchmarks supports complementarity rather than complete replacement by one tool: the two
types of tools may find different vulnerabilities and may also produce different kinds of false positives [1,15].

7.2    Comparison of Different LLM Methods
   Prompting, fine-tuning, structural enhancement, and multi-model collaboration solve different problems.
Prompting lowers the adaptation threshold, fine-tuning improves output stability, structural enhancement
supplements program dependencies, and collaboration uses model differences. GRACE, DLAP, context
enhancement, and M2CVD all report gains in their own settings, but datasets, model versions, and evaluation
protocols differ, so they cannot be directly ranked on this basis [11-13,29]. Comprehensive benchmark studies
also show that preprocessing and prompt changes alter model rankings [26,31].
    Table V in PrimeVul compares five code language models. When trained and tested on BigVul, F1 is
62.88%-68.26%. When BigVul-trained models are transferred to PRIMEVUL testing, F1 drops to 1.91%-
5.82%. When PRIMEVUL is used for both training and testing, F1 rises to 18.05%-21.43% [14]. Under the
strict setting, VD-S is 88.78%-91.51%, both paired functions are correct in only 1.06%-3.01% of cases, and
both are judged safe in 84.22%-88.30% of cases. The above decline is not an isolated case of StarCoder2, but
the conclusion is limited to the five models and three settings in Table V.

7.3    Cost and Deployment Choices
   Deployment plans depend on whether code can be sent outside, whether the task is stable, whether context
depends on cross-function or tool evidence, and the false-positive and computation costs that an organization
can bear. Sensitive code and local large-scale scanning are usually more suitable for lightweight models or
----
=== [PDF page 14] ===
                      zeuspress.org; Computers and Artificial Intelligence; Volume 3 · Issue 5 · 2026
performance improvements on specific benchmarks, but the related conclusions are affected by label quality,
duplicate samples, data splitting, evaluation metrics, and model versions.
   Therefore, evaluation cannot remain at a single F1 score. It is also necessary to examine whether the data
are independent, whether task granularity is consistent with the label source, whether the results remain stable
under cross-project and out-of-time settings, and whether the costs caused by false positives, localization, and
explanation are acceptable. Existing evidence better supports a complementary relationship among LLMs,
SAST, and human auditing, rather than replacing the complete security process with a single model. Only
when method design advances together with data governance and strict evaluation can advantages on
benchmarks be transformed into auditable and reproducible engineering capability.

29:- [A] A head-to-head quantitative and qualitative evaluation of three rule-based SAST tools (SonarQube, CodeQL, Snyk Code) and three LLMs on the GitHub Models platform (GPT-4.1, Mistral Large, DeepSeek V3) for vulnerability detection, measuring precision, recall, F1, latency and developer effort (p. 1–2).
51:- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] TP = reported finding matching a known vulnerability (manually verified); FP = reported − TP; FN = known − TP; precision, recall and F1 computed per project and then averaged across projects (p. 6–7, p. 10). [V] Exception: for LLMs, wrong line/column locations were not counted against them (p. 6). [V] FP ratio (share of a tool's reports that are false) shown in Fig. 4 (p. 9). [V] Execution time per run (p. 7, p. 9).
55:1. [V] Mean precision / recall / F1 (macro over 10 projects): SonarQube 0.567 / 0.187 / 0.260; CodeQL 0.625 / 0.284 / 0.386; Snyk Code 0.686 / 0.523 / 0.546; GPT-4.1 0.757 / 0.877 / 0.797; Mistral Large 0.783 / 0.783 / 0.753; DeepSeek V3 0.723 / 0.847 / 0.750 (Table 13, p. 10).
56:2. [V] Raw counts (reported / TP over 63 known vulnerabilities): SonarQube 15 / 13; CodeQL 26 / 21; Snyk Code 57 / 42; GPT-4.1 74 / 55; Mistral Large 61 / 48; DeepSeek V3 70 / 52 (summed from Tables 4–5, p. 8). [I] Pooled over all projects this gives precision/recall/F1 of about 0.87/0.21/0.33 (SonarQube), 0.81/0.33/0.47 (CodeQL), 0.74/0.67/0.70 (Snyk), 0.74/0.87/0.80 (GPT-4.1), 0.79/0.76/0.77 (Mistral), 0.74/0.83/0.78 (DeepSeek) — our arithmetic from Tables 4–5; pooled SAST precision is higher than the macro averages suggest.
74:- [I] Averaging choice penalises SAST: projects where a tool reports nothing get precision 0.000 and are averaged in (p. 9). Pooled counts (our calculation from Tables 4–5, p. 8) give SAST precision 0.74–0.87 vs LLM 0.74–0.79, and Snyk pooled F1 ≈ 0.70 near the LLMs. The FP-ratio ranking (DeepSeek highest) also depends on per-project averaging; pooled, GPT-4.1 has the most FPs (19) and Snyk's FP share (15/57) is similar to the LLMs'.
85:- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] N = 10 projects, 63 vulns, single runs, no tests or CIs; per-project F1 varies widely (e.g., S04 with 1 vulnerability).
94:- How it informs our work [I]: A rare head-to-head comparison of commercial-grade SAST with frontier LLMs, reporting full precision/recall/F1 and runtime, in an under-studied language (C#). Its LLM-favourable result is useful but rests on a tiny, purpose-built benchmark and asymmetric scoring, so it should be treated as weak evidence and contrasted with larger real-world studies.

1	---
     2	key: lu2025lab
     3	status: ready
     4	evidence_basis: full-text
     5	design: empirical evaluation; within/cross-dataset DL training + temporally separated OOD test of DL and off-the-shelf open-weight LLMs
     6	dataset: Juliet, Devign, BigVul, ICVul (train/test); VentiVul (new; Linux+Chromium CVEs disclosed from 2025-05-01) for OOD
     7	sample_size: 4 DL models x 4 datasets; VentiVul 13,326 functions, 200 CVEs, 263 vulnerable-patched pairs; 4 LLMs x 3 prompts
     8	metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1; CVE Detection Rate (CDR); Patch Pair Accuracy (PACC); t-SNE centroid distance
     9	main_finding: DL F1 up to 91-94.5 in-distribution falls to 3.47-8.65 on temporally separated VentiVul; open-weight LLMs reach only 0.79-5.36 conservative F1; PACC <6% for all.
    10	relevance: high
    11	analysed: 2026-11-12
    12	---
    13	<!-- Frontmatter: single-line values; they feed literature-matrix.md via `rlab index`.
    14	     status: draft (in progress) -> ready (analyst self-check passed) -> complete (critical review passed).
    15	     evidence_basis: full-text | abstract-only. abstract-only analyses must not fill methodology detail.
    16	     relevance: high | medium | low. -->
    17	
    18	# From Lab to Reality: A Practical Evaluation of Deep Learning Models and LLMs for Vulnerability Detection
    19	
    20	- Authors: Lu, Chaomeng; Lagaisse, Bert
    21	- Year / venue: 2025, arXiv (preprint)
    22	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2512.10485 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.10485
    23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
    24	
    25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
    26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
    27	
    28	## 1. Research objective
    29	- [A] Test whether DL vulnerability detectors and LLMs that score well on curated benchmarks still work under deployment-like conditions. The study looks at three things: separability of code representations, within- vs cross-dataset generalisation, and detection of recent, temporally separated vulnerabilities (p. 1, p. 2).
    30	- [A] Contribution claimed: VentiVul, a temporally separated out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmark of 200 CVEs / 263 vulnerable–patched pairs, plus a "Whole-File" + "Function-Pair" evaluation protocol (p. 2). "Out-of-distribution" means test data drawn from a different source or period than the training data.
    31	
    32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
    33	- [A] RQ1: do graph-based and CodeBERT representations separate vulnerable from non-vulnerable code before task-specific training? (p. 6)
    34	- [A] RQ2: how do benchmark characteristics affect within-dataset and cross-dataset performance of DL detectors? (p. 7)
    35	- [A] RQ3: how well do trained DL models and off-the-shelf LLMs detect recent vulnerabilities on a temporally separated benchmark? (p. 7)
    36	- No formal hypotheses.
    37	
    38	## 3. Methodology
    39	- Research design: [V] Controlled empirical evaluation in three stages: representation diagnostics (t-SNE + centroid distance), 4×4 train/test matrix of DL models across datasets, inference-only evaluation on VentiVul (pp. 6–8).
    40	- Approach / models: [V] DL: Devign (gated GNN on code property graphs), ReVeal (Joern graphs + token embeddings, SMOTE), LineVul (fine-tuned CodeBERT), VulBERTa (RoBERTa pretrained on C/C++) (p. 5). LLMs, open-weight, no fine-tuning: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct (16B MoE, 2.4B active), Qwen3-30B-A3B (thinking mode disabled), Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501, all released before May 2025 (p. 5, p. 8).
    41	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] DL vs LLM only on VentiVul. Only ReVeal and LineVul (each trained on the four datasets) were taken to VentiVul; Devign and VulBERTa were not (p. 7). LLM prompting: zero-shot, few-shot (k=4, two complete pairs), chain-of-thought (p. 8, Table 4 p. 9). [I] No SAST tool, no proprietary/frontier LLM, no fine-tuned LLM and no trivial baseline (e.g. all-positive or random) is included.
    42	
    43	## 4. Dataset and sample
    44	- Data source(s): [V] Juliet 253,002 functions, 37% vulnerable, synthetic; Devign 27,318, 46%, manual; BigVul 188,636, 6%, patches; ICVul 15,396, 41%, patches (p. 3, Table 1). All C/C++.
    45	- VentiVul: [V] CVEs for Linux and Chromium disclosed from May 1, 2025, taken from NVD in disclosure order until 100 per project; manually verified; target size fixed before collection; "records were not selected based on model predictions" (p. 4). 13,326 functions, 200 CVEs, 39 CWEs, 263 pairs; Chromium 7,095 functions / 100 CVEs / 20 CWEs / 147 pairs; Linux 6,231 / 100 / 27 / 116 (p. 4, Table 2). Pre-fix function = vulnerable, post-fix = non-vulnerable, plus other functions from the same files labelled non-vulnerable to keep realistic imbalance (p. 4).
    46	- Sample size (N) and unit: functions (Whole-File), CVEs (CDR) and vulnerable–patched pairs (PACC) (p. 7). [I] With 263 vulnerable functions in 13,326, VentiVul prevalence is about 2.0%. We infer this from p. 4; the paper does not state the positive count for Whole-File.
    47	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Inclusion: valid references, explicit fix in non-test C/C++ files, CWE available; excluded: missing references, non-C/C++ or test-only fixes, fixes with "excessive unrelated files or functions" (p. 4). Train/test split ratios for the four benchmarks: not reported.
    48	- Data availability: [V] "All of our datasets, code, and results are available" on GitHub (p. 2).
    49	
    50	## 5. Experimental setup
    51	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] DL models use the original authors' code and "recommended settings" (p. 8); H100 GPUs (p. 8). Leakage controls: strict train–test splits with duplicate functions filtered, a fixed test set per target benchmark (p. 7). LLMs run locally via vLLM on B200 GPUs, temperature 0, top-p 1, seed 42, max 384 output tokens, JSON-only binary label; unparseable outputs kept as failures (p. 8). Each model, DL or LLM, receives one function at a time (p. 7, p. 8). Few-shot demonstrations are removed from the test set by pair identifier and code hash (p. 8). ReVeal metrics are computed only over functions its preprocessing can handle (p. 7). Two policies for LLMs: valid-only and conservative (failures counted wrong) (p. 8).
    52	- Code availability: [V] public GitHub repository (p. 2).
    53	
    54	## 6. Evaluation metrics
    55	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 for Whole-File (p. 9). CVE Detection Rate (CDR): share of CVEs with at least one vulnerable function flagged, i.e. CVE-level coverage (p. 9). Patch Pair Accuracy (PACC): share of pairs where the vulnerable version is flagged and the patched version is not, i.e. sensitivity to the fix (p. 9). Centroid distance in min-max normalised t-SNE space, described as descriptive only (pp. 8–9).
    56	- Statistical testing: not reported. There are no significance tests, confidence intervals or repeated runs; LLMs use one deterministic run (p. 8) and DL results come from single training runs (seeds for DL not reported).
    57	
    58	## 7. Key findings
    59	1. In-distribution DL (within-dataset) — [V] LineVul F1 94.52 and VulBERTa 94.14 on Juliet; LineVul F1 91.00 on BigVul (p. 11; Table 6 p. 12). On BigVul, ReVeal, Devign and VulBERTa reach accuracy 87.45, 94.09, 94.39 but F1 only 23.58, 16.90, 0.19 (p. 11). Accuracy is therefore misleading at 6% prevalence.
    60	2. Cross-dataset DL — [V] LineVul (Juliet) F1 94.52 in-dataset falls to 53.95 (Devign), 10.73 (BigVul), 51.22 (ICVul) (p. 11). LineVul (BigVul) falls from 91.00 to 0 (Juliet), 1.90 (Devign), 13.05 (ICVul) (p. 12). ReVeal (BigVul) is below 1.00 F1 on all three external sets (p. 11). [A] "No evaluated model consistently preserves its within-dataset performance" (p. 11).
    61	3. Temporally separated DL (VentiVul, Whole-File) — [V] F1 3.47–8.65 across the 8 ReVeal/LineVul configurations; best ReVeal (BigVul) F1 8.65 with precision 5.25%, recall 24.43% (p. 13, Table 7). Devign-trained models: recall 99.24–100% but precision about 2% (p. 13, Table 7). LineVul (BigVul) F1 6.87 on VentiVul vs 91.00 in-distribution (Table 7 p. 13; Table 6 p. 12).
    62	4. Temporally separated LLMs (VentiVul) — [V] Conservative F1 0.79–5.36 across 4 models × 3 prompts; all conservative F1 < 5.5% and all PACC < 6% (p. 13; Table 8 p. 14). Best: Mistral-Small-24B few-shot F1 5.36%, CDR 46%, PACC 5.75% (p. 13). Highest valid-only F1: Qwen2.5-Coder-32B CoT 8.21% (conservative 3.04%) (p. 14, Table 8). Zero-shot conservative F1: Qwen2.5-Coder 3.72, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite 4.29, Qwen3 3.09, Mistral 4.07 (p. 14, Table 8). LLM precision and recall are not reported, and the LLMs have no in-distribution numbers.
    63	5. DL vs LLM on the same OOD data [V/I] — best DL F1 8.65 (ReVeal-BigVul) vs best LLM conservative F1 5.36 (Mistral few-shot) (p. 13; p. 14). Zero-shot LLM CDR (34%, 20%, 9%, 5%) is lower than most DL configurations (p. 13). Best PACC: DL 5.34% vs LLM 5.75% (p. 13). [I] Both families are close to an all-positive predictor at ~2% prevalence (F1 ≈ 3.9%, our calculation from p. 4 counts); LineVul (Devign) at recall 100%, precision 2%, F1 3.93 is effectively that predictor (p. 13, Table 7).
    64	6. CDR vs PACC gap — [V] ReVeal (Devign), ReVeal (ICVul), LineVul (Devign) reach CDR 99.10%, 94.59%, 100% but PACC 0.76%, 0%, 0% (p. 13). [A] Detecting a vulnerable function "does not imply" telling it apart from its patch (p. 13).
    65	7. Prompting — [V] Few-shot improves Mistral on all three metrics but degrades the other models; CoT raises Qwen2.5-Coder valid-only F1 but lowers its PACC (p. 13). [A] Prompting effects are "model- and metric-dependent" (p. 13).
    66	8. Project/CWE variation — [V] All LLMs have higher CDR on Linux than Chromium. DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite zero-shot CDR is 26% on Chromium and 42% on Linux (p. 13). LineVul (BigVul) has CDR 76% on Chromium and 0 on Linux (p. 13). Best project-specific PACC is < 8% (LineVul-ICVul 7.48% on Chromium) (p. 14). Per-CWE PACC peaks at 18.18% (LineVul-ICVul, CWE-472) on small cells (p. 14).
    67	9. Representations — [V] GNN centroid distances: Juliet 0.0242, ICVul 0.0057, BigVul 0.1612; CodeBERT: BigVul 0.166, Devign 0.0068 (pp. 9–10). [A] Neither representation consistently separates vulnerable from non-vulnerable code (p. 10).
    68	
    69	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
    70	- [A] Only four DL models, two DL families on VentiVul, four open-weight LLMs; no proprietary LLMs; conclusions apply to the evaluated models (p. 17).
    71	- [A] LLM pretraining corpora and cutoffs are unknown, so temporal separation "cannot fully exclude training-data contamination" (p. 17).
    72	- [A] t-SNE is parameter-sensitive, and centroid distance cannot capture nonlinear structure. RQ1 does not establish a causal link to RQ2/RQ3 performance (p. 17, p. 15).
    73	- [A] Dataset characteristics vary simultaneously, so individual causes cannot be isolated. Preprocessing drops some functions, which affects comparability (p. 17).
    74	- [A] VentiVul is C/C++ only (Linux, Chromium) and may not generalise to other languages or proprietary code. "Unrelated" functions may hide other vulnerabilities (residual label noise), and regex function extraction can miss complex C/C++ syntax, which mainly affects Whole-File (p. 17).
    75	
    76	## 9. Limitations we identified
    77	- [I] No trivial baseline. At ~2% prevalence an all-positive classifier scores F1 ≈ 3.9%, so most reported DL and LLM F1 values (3.09–8.65) are at or barely above chance. The paper describes them as "low" but never compares them with chance.
    78	- [I] The DL and LLM comparison is asymmetric. DL models were trained on historical data; LLMs were used zero/few-shot without fine-tuning, with small open-weight models (MoE models with 2.4–3B active parameters) and Qwen3 thinking disabled (p. 5, p. 8). The study says nothing about frontier or fine-tuned LLMs, and nothing about LLMs in-distribution, because LLMs were not run on the four benchmarks.
    79	- [I] LLM precision/recall are not reported (Table 8 gives F1, CDR, PACC only, p. 14), so we cannot tell whether LLMs fail through false positives or false negatives.
    80	- [I] Single run, no confidence intervals; with 263 pairs, PACC differences of a few points (e.g. 5.34% vs 5.75%) are within noise.
    81	- [I] One function at a time with no context (p. 7). This is fair between families but disadvantages LLMs, which may need inter-procedural context. Many Linux/Chromium bugs need cross-function reasoning (cf. CVE-2025-37777 spanning two files, p. 4).
    82	- [I] No static-analysis tool is evaluated, although the introduction positions learning-based detection as a complement to static analysis (p. 1).
    83	- [I] Preprint status: arXiv v4 dated 4 Nov 2026 carries a footnote "accepted for publication in the Journal of Systems and Software" (p. 1). Acceptance is author-stated; no journal DOI is in metadata.
    84	
    85	## 10. Threats to validity
    86	- Internal: [I] Deduplication within datasets and fixed test sets are reported (p. 7), but split ratios and cross-dataset overlap checks are not reported (Devign is from FFmpeg/QEMU and BigVul from open-source C/C++ repositories, p. 3, so project overlap is possible but unchecked). ReVeal is scored only on functions it can process (p. 7), which may inflate or deflate its numbers relative to LineVul.
    87	- External: [I] C/C++, two very large projects, 200 CVEs, open-weight mid-size LLMs only (p. 4, p. 5).
    88	- Construct: [I] Labelling unrelated same-file functions as non-vulnerable (p. 4) is a realistic construct for "scan the whole file", though label noise remains (p. 17). PACC is a strict and useful measure of patch sensitivity. CDR rewards indiscriminate positive prediction, as the paper itself shows (p. 13).
    89	- Statistical conclusion: [I] No tests, single runs, small per-CWE cells (p. 14).
    90	- Reproducibility: [I] Good: data, code and results are public (p. 2), and decoding settings and prompts are fully given (p. 8, p. 9). DL hyper-parameters are given only by reference to the original implementations (p. 8).
    91	
    92	## 11. Future research directions
    93	- Stated by authors [A]: representations and training that emphasise security-relevant changes, e.g. vulnerable–patched pair supervision (p. 16); datasets prioritising reliable labels, diverse patterns and explicit vulnerability–fix links over size (p. 16); complementing within-dataset evaluation with cross-dataset and temporally separated testing, and reporting CDR and patch-pair metrics with function-level metrics (p. 16); studying individual dataset factors, broader ecosystems and "more advanced LLM adaptation strategies" (p. 16).
    94	- Suggested by us [I]: run SAST tools and frontier/fine-tuned LLMs on VentiVul with file/repository context and a chance baseline. That would give exactly the same-benchmark LLM vs SAST vs DL comparison our RQ5 identifies as missing.
    95	
    96	## 12. Relevance to our research
    97	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (DL vs LLM on same OOD data), RQ2 (temporal separation, cross-dataset shift, class ratio, accuracy vs F1), RQ4 (per-project and per-CWE variation, C/C++), RQ5 (patch-pair sensitivity, chance baselines).
    98	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the strongest direct evidence in our set that in-distribution DL scores (F1 91–94.5) do not survive temporal and dataset shift (F1 3.5–8.7). Off-the-shelf mid-size LLMs do no better than the shifted DL detectors, and both sit near chance. It supports the RQ2 claim that evaluation setup drives the reported ranking, and agrees with the PrimeVul near-random pair results (ding2025vulnerability). It covers no SAST tool or cost, so it adds nothing for RQ3.
    99	
   100	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
   101	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
   102	|---|---|---|---|---|
   103	| RQ2 | In-distribution DL F1 is high (LineVul 94.52 Juliet, 91.00 BigVul; VulBERTa 94.14 Juliet) but drops cross-dataset (LineVul-BigVul → 0 / 1.90 / 13.05; LineVul-Juliet → 53.95 / 10.73 / 51.22) | 11, 12 | V | moderate (preprint, single run, 4 models) |
   104	| RQ2 | High accuracy hides failure at 6% prevalence: BigVul accuracy 87.45/94.09/94.39 with F1 23.58/16.90/0.19 (ReVeal/Devign/VulBERTa) | 11 | V | moderate |
   105	| RQ1 | On temporally separated VentiVul (CVEs from May 2025, ~2% prevalence), trained DL F1 3.47–8.65 (best ReVeal-BigVul 8.65, P 5.25%) | 13 | V | moderate |
   106	| RQ1 | On the same VentiVul functions, 4 open-weight LLMs (zero/few-shot/CoT) reach conservative F1 0.79–5.36 (best Mistral-24B few-shot), PACC < 6%; zero-shot CDR 5–34%, below most DL configs | 13, 14 | V | moderate |
   107	| RQ1 | Both families are close to an all-positive baseline (F1 ≈ 3.9% at ~2% prevalence); no family is practically usable on recent CVEs | 4, 13 | I | moderate (our calculation from reported counts) |
   108	| RQ2 | High CVE-level coverage does not mean patch sensitivity: CDR 94.59–100% with PACC 0–0.76% for Devign/ICVul-trained models; all DL PACC < 5.5% | 13 | V | moderate |
   109	| RQ4 | Results vary by project and CWE: LineVul-BigVul CDR 76% Chromium vs 0% Linux; all LLMs higher CDR on Linux; best per-CWE PACC 18.18% (CWE-472) on small cells | 13, 14 | V | weak (small cells) |
   110	| RQ2 | Prompting effects are model- and metric-dependent: few-shot helps only Mistral; CoT raises Qwen2.5 valid-only F1 but lowers PACC | 13 | V | weak |
   111	| RQ5 | Temporal separation by release date cannot exclude LLM training contamination; unrelated-function labels carry residual noise | 17 | A | moderate |
   112	
   113	## 14. Key quotes
   114	> "When evaluated on VentiVul, performance drops sharply, with most models failing to detect vulnerabilities reliably or distinguish vulnerable functions from their patched counterparts." (p. 1)
   115	
   116	> "All conservative F1-scores remain below 5.5%, and all PACC values remain below 6%." (p. 13)
   117	
   118	> "This manuscript has been accepted for publication in the Journal of Systems and Software." (p. 1)
   119	
   120	## Analyst notes
   121	- Reading coverage: all 20 PDF pages read, including references. Figures 3–7 (t-SNE plots, per-project and per-CWE bar charts, pp. 10–16) are images. Their key numbers were taken from the results text, which quotes them; we did not read bar heights.
   122	- Venue status [I]: `venue_kind: preprint` (arXiv 2512.10485v4, 4 Nov 2026, p. 1). The PDF footnote states acceptance at Journal of Systems and Software (p. 1), but no JSS DOI/version was found in metadata. Treat it as "not peer-reviewed (author-reported JSS acceptance)" until a published version is added via `rlab add`. If the published version appears, it should replace this one.
   123	- Metadata mismatch [I]: `metadata.json` `added_reason` mentions "RQ2 label quality vs family (WordPress PHP)" and "G6 cost/energy at realistic prevalence". This paper contains no PHP/WordPress data and no cost or energy measurement (C/C++ only, p. 3, p. 4; no cost reporting found by grep). Those motivations apply to a different paper; this one supports G2 (temporal OOD DL vs LLM) only.
   124	- Uncertainties: the exact number of vulnerable functions in the Whole-File set (we assume 263, one per pair). Train/test split ratios for the four benchmarks are not reported. ReVeal's VentiVul coverage (functions dropped by preprocessing) is not quantified.

key: chakraborty2024revisiting
status: complete

design: Replication + re-evaluation of 4 DL detectors (and 2 fine-tuned LLMs) on a new whole-project, time-split dataset (Real-Vul)

relevance: high
analysed: 2026-11-12

input.old_string: - How it informs our work [I]: This is the strongest direct evidence in our set that in-distribution DL scores (F1 91–94.5) do not survive temporal and dataset shift (F1 3.5–8.7). Off-the-shelf mid-size LLMs do no better than the shifted DL detectors, and both sit near chance. It supports the RQ2 claim that evaluation setup drives the reported ranking, and agrees with the PrimeVul near-random pair results (ding2025vulnerability).
input.new_string: - How it informs our work [I]: This is direct, peer-reviewed (JSS 2026) evidence that in-distribution DL scores do not survive temporal shift. It is consistent with ding2025vulnerability, which shows BigVul-trained models collapse on PrimeVul [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 7]. LineVul's F1 falls from 91–94.5 in-distribution (p. 12) to 4.39–6.87 on VentiVul, and all 8 DL configurations score 3.47–8.65 (p. 13). On F1, the evaluated open-weight LLMs (≤ 32B) do no better than the shifted DL detectors (0.79–5.36), and both families sit within a few points of the all-positive F1 of ≈ 3.87%. On PACC, both families are far below the random q(1−q) level (up to 25%), i.e. they rarely tell a function apart from its patch. It supports the RQ2 claim that evaluation setup drives the reported ranking.

input.new_string: - Sample size (N) and unit: functions (Whole-File), CVEs (CDR) and vulnerable–patched pairs (PACC) (p. 7). [I] Each of the 263 pairs has exactly one vulnerable function (p. 4), so prevalence p = 263/13,326 = 1.97%. The Table 7 numbers confirm this: back-calculating prevalence from accuracy, precision and recall gives 1.97% for every LineVul row, which matches 263/13,326. The ReVeal rows give 1.79%, because ReVeal is scored only on the functions its preprocessing can handle (p. 7). An all-positive classifier would therefore score F1 = 2p/(1+p) ≈ 3.87% on the full set and ≈ 3.5% on ReVeal's subset (our calculation from p. 4 and Table 7 p. 13).

input.old_string: 5. DL vs LLM on the same OOD data [V/I] — best DL F1 8.65 (ReVeal-BigVul) vs best LLM conservative F1 5.36 (Mistral few-shot) (p. 13; p. 14). Zero-shot LLM CDR (34%, 20%, 9%, 5%) is lower than most DL configurations (p. 13). Best PACC: DL 5.34% vs LLM 5.75% (p. 13). [I] Both families are close to an all-positive predictor at ~2% prevalence (F1 ≈ 3.9%, our calculation from p. 4 counts); LineVul (Devign) at recall 100%, precision 2%, F1 3.93 is effectively that predictor (p. 13, Table 7).
input.new_string: 5. DL vs LLM on VentiVul (mostly but not exactly the same samples) [V/I] — [V] best DL Whole-File F1 8.65 (ReVeal-BigVul) vs best LLM conservative F1 5.36 (Mistral few-shot) (p. 13; p. 14). Zero-shot LLM CDR (34%, 20%, 9%, 5%) is lower than most DL configurations (p. 13). Best PACC: DL 5.34% vs LLM 5.75% (p. 13). [V] The evaluated samples differ: ReVeal is scored only on functions it can process (p. 7), the few-shot test set excludes pairs used as demonstrations, and valid-only metrics use only parseable outputs (p. 8). [I] F1 against chance (all-positive F1 ≈ 3.87% at p = 1.97%; ≈ 3.5% on ReVeal's subset; §4): the best DL F1 of 8.65 is about 2.5× its chance level, while the best LLM F1 of 5.36 is about 1.4× chance. LineVul (Devign), with recall 100%, precision 2% and F1 3.93, is in effect the all-positive predictor (p. 13, Table 7). [I] PACC against chance: a random labeller that flags a fraction q of functions independently of their content would get PACC = q(1−q), up to 25% at q = 0.5. All observed PACC values (≤ 5.75%, DL and LLM) are far below that, which means the models usually give the vulnerable and the patched version the same label (our reasoning from the PACC definition, p. 9). This matches ding2025vulnerability, where random pair-wise correctness is 22.70% and models fall far below it [@ding2025vulnerability, p. 9].
